chunks.title: Bond taxation lifecycle
sample_questions: How are bonds taxed across their lifecycle?
When do I pay tax on bonds?
What tax applies when I receive interest or sell a bond?
chunks.chunk: Bond taxation generally happens at three stages: when interest is received, when the bond is sold before maturity, and when a bond purchased at a premium or discount is redeemed at maturity. Interest is normally taxed as income from other sources. Selling or redeeming a bond can create a capital gain or capital loss depending on the purchase cost, sale value or maturity value, and holding period.
chunks.answer_guidance: Give a simple lifecycle view: interest payout is taxed separately from capital gain or loss. Avoid personal tax advice and suggest consulting a tax professional for individual filing decisions.

chunks.title: Interest is taxed when paid or credited
sample_questions: Is accrued interest taxable?
When is bond interest taxed?
Is the interest shown on the platform taxable immediately?
chunks.chunk: Bond interest is taxed when it is actually paid or credited by the issuing entity, not merely because the platform shows daily accrued interest. The platform may show accrued interest for tracking, but tax usually applies when the coupon payout happens or when accrued interest is settled as part of a sale before maturity.
chunks.answer_guidance: Clarify the difference between displayed accrual and actual interest received. State that taxable interest is reported under income from other sources.

chunks.title: Accrued interest example
sample_questions: If accrued interest is higher than received interest, what is taxable?
How much interest should I report if only part was paid?
Can you explain accrued versus received interest with an example?
chunks.chunk: If the platform shows accrued interest of Rs. 4,300 but the user actually receives Rs. 3,000 as interest, the taxable interest for that payout is Rs. 3,000. The displayed accrued amount by itself does not mean the entire amount has become taxable immediately.
chunks.answer_guidance: Use numbers to explain that tax follows the actual interest received or credited. Keep the answer practical for investor relations support.

chunks.title: TDS on bond interest
sample_questions: When is TDS deducted on bond interest?
Which section applies to TDS on bonds?
Why was TDS deducted from my interest payout?
chunks.chunk: TDS on bond interest is deducted when interest is paid. The PDF notes Section 193 for interest on securities until 31 March 2026 and Section 393 from 1 April 2026. TDS reduces the net amount paid to the user, but the user must still report the gross interest income while filing ITR and claim the deducted TDS as tax credit where applicable.
chunks.answer_guidance: Explain that TDS is a tax credit, not the final tax calculation. Mention section references only as general information and avoid legal certainty for individual cases.

chunks.title: TDS threshold does not remove tax liability
sample_questions: Why was no TDS deducted on my bond interest?
If TDS is not deducted, is the interest tax free?
What is the Rs. 10,000 TDS rule?
chunks.chunk: TDS may not be deducted if the interest paid by an issuer is below the applicable threshold, commonly Rs. 10,000 depending on issuer type and compliance rules. However, absence of TDS does not make the interest tax-free. The interest income may still need to be reported in the user’s ITR.
chunks.answer_guidance: Separate TDS deduction from income tax liability. Say that the issuer's threshold and compliance process can affect whether TDS is deducted.

chunks.title: Gross interest reporting when TDS is deducted
sample_questions: Should I report gross or net interest in ITR?
If I receive interest after TDS, what amount is taxable?
How do I claim TDS credit?
chunks.chunk: If interest is Rs. 20,000, TDS is Rs. 2,000, and the user receives Rs. 18,000, the user should generally report the gross interest amount of Rs. 20,000 in ITR. The Rs. 2,000 deducted can be claimed as TDS credit, subject to the user's tax computation and reflected tax records.
chunks.answer_guidance: Use the gross-interest example from the PDF. Remind the user to reconcile TDS credit before filing.

chunks.title: Capital gains calculation on bonds
sample_questions: How is capital gain calculated on bonds?
What creates a capital loss in bonds?
Is profit on selling a bond taxed as capital gains?
chunks.chunk: Capital gain or loss is based on the difference between the investment amount or acquisition cost and the selling amount or maturity amount. If the sale or redemption amount is higher than the purchase cost, it is a capital gain. If it is lower, it is a capital loss. Interest received is taxed separately from capital gain or loss.
chunks.answer_guidance: Explain the broad formula and keep interest taxation separate from capital gains taxation.

chunks.title: Holding period and tax rate for listed bonds
sample_questions: What is the holding period for listed bonds?
What tax rate applies if I sell bonds after one year?
How are STCG and LTCG taxed on bonds?
chunks.chunk: For listed bonds, the PDF states that holdings below 12 months are treated as short-term capital gains and taxed at the investor's applicable slab rate. Holdings over 12 months are treated as long-term capital gains and taxed at 12.5% based on Budget 2024 changes. The PDF notes no minimum exemption threshold for LTCG on bonds, so the 12.5% rate applies to the full gain.
chunks.answer_guidance: State the short-term versus long-term distinction clearly. Avoid applying the rule to unlisted instruments unless separately verified.

chunks.title: Capital gain and interest are taxed separately
sample_questions: Are interest and capital gains combined for tax?
How is tax calculated if I sell a bond and also receive interest?
Can you give a bond sale tax example?
chunks.chunk: If a user invests Rs. 50,000, sells the bond for Rs. 54,000, and receives Rs. 1,000 as interest, the Rs. 4,000 difference is treated as capital gain while the Rs. 1,000 interest is taxed separately as interest income under income from other sources.
chunks.answer_guidance: Use this example to prevent mixing interest income with capital gains.

chunks.title: Capital loss set-off and carry forward
sample_questions: Can I set off capital loss from bonds?
How long can capital loss be carried forward?
Can long-term capital loss offset short-term capital gain?
chunks.chunk: Short-term capital loss can be set off against both short-term and long-term capital gains. Long-term capital loss can be set off only against long-term capital gains, not short-term capital gains. Unused capital loss can be carried forward for 8 years if it is declared in the ITR as required.
chunks.answer_guidance: Mention STCL and LTCL rules separately. Encourage proper ITR reporting for carry-forward eligibility.

chunks.title: Maturity taxation for regular bonds
sample_questions: What is taxed when my bond matures?
Is principal repayment taxable at maturity?
How is maturity redemption treated for tax?
chunks.chunk: At maturity, the bond's face value or principal is returned. For a regular bond, only the interest component is taxed as interest income. Principal repayment is generally a return of capital, but a bond purchased at a premium or discount can still create a capital loss or gain on redemption.
chunks.answer_guidance: Keep the standard maturity case simple, then mention premium or discount as the exception that can affect capital gain or loss.

chunks.title: Bonds purchased at premium
sample_questions: What happens if I buy a bond above face value?
Why do I see capital loss on a premium bond?
Can premium paid on a bond create capital loss?
chunks.chunk: A bond purchased above face value can create a capital loss at maturity. For example, if the investment amount is Rs. 1,01,000 and maturity value is Rs. 1,00,000, the Rs. 1,000 difference is treated as capital loss. Interest earned on the bond remains taxable separately as income from other sources.
chunks.answer_guidance: Explain that premium impacts the capital gains or loss calculation, while coupon interest remains taxable separately.

chunks.title: Bonds purchased at discount
sample_questions: What happens if I buy a bond below face value?
Is discount on bond redemption taxable?
Why is there a capital gain at maturity?
chunks.chunk: A bond purchased below face value can create a capital gain at maturity. For example, if the investment amount is Rs. 90,000 and the bond matures at Rs. 1,00,000, the Rs. 10,000 difference is treated as capital gain, subject to applicable holding period rules.
chunks.answer_guidance: Give the discount-to-face-value example and connect it to capital gains treatment.

chunks.title: Deep discount and zero coupon bonds
sample_questions: How are zero coupon bonds taxed?
What is tax treatment for deep discount bonds?
What happens if I sell a zero coupon bond before maturity?
chunks.chunk: For deep discount or zero coupon bonds, the PDF states that if held till maturity, TDS may apply and the repayment income is considered income from other sources taxed at slab rate. If sold after holding for more than one year and before maturity, the income may be considered a long-term capital gain taxed at 12.5%, subject to the specific bond and applicable rules.
chunks.answer_guidance: Treat zero coupon/deep discount bonds as a special case and avoid overgeneralizing. Suggest professional tax review for specific instruments.

chunks.title: TDS lifecycle and Form 168 reflection
sample_questions: How does TDS reach Form 168?
Why is TDS not visible immediately?
What is the TDS reporting lifecycle?
chunks.chunk: The TDS lifecycle is: the issuer deducts TDS, pays net interest to the user, deposits TDS with the government, files the quarterly TDS return, and then the Income Tax Department processes the data. TDS generally reflects in Form 168, previously Form 26AS, around 10 to 15 days after the filing due date is completed. A delay in Form 168 does not always mean the TDS is missing.
chunks.answer_guidance: Use the step-by-step lifecycle to calm mismatch concerns. Emphasize quarterly processing timelines.

chunks.title: Form 168 shows TDS credit, not total income
sample_questions: What does Form 168 show for bonds?
Does Form 168 show my total bond income?
Why must I declare income separately if TDS is visible?
chunks.chunk: Form 168, previously Form 26AS, shows TDS deducted and reported against the user's PAN. It does not necessarily show the user's total taxable bond income. The user must declare income separately in ITR and use the reflected TDS as tax credit, if available.
chunks.answer_guidance: Distinguish TDS credit reporting from income reporting. Mention PAN linkage and reconciliation.

chunks.title: Claiming TDS while filing ITR
sample_questions: How do I claim TDS on bond interest?
Can TDS be adjusted against my final tax?
Where is TDS used while filing ITR?
chunks.chunk: Users can claim or set off deducted TDS while filing their Income Tax Return. During filing, the user reports total taxable income, the tax liability is calculated, and TDS already deducted is adjusted against the final payable tax. The TDS amount should be reconciled with Form 168 or other tax credit records.
chunks.answer_guidance: Explain the claim process at a high level and avoid filing the user's return in the response.

chunks.title: Form 121 replaces Form 15G and 15H from FY 2026-27
sample_questions: What is Form 121?
Does Form 121 replace Form 15G and 15H?
Why submit Form 121 for bond interest?
chunks.chunk: The PDF says the Government has proposed a unified declaration form, Form 121, replacing both Form 15G and Form 15H from FY 2026-27. The purpose remains to declare that total income is below the taxable limit so that TDS is not deducted on interest income. The new form is described as age-neutral and intended to simplify compliance.
chunks.answer_guidance: Use cautious wording such as 'the PDF states' or 'proposed' because this is future-facing compliance information.

chunks.title: Reconciling bond income and TDS
sample_questions: How should I reconcile bond TDS?
What documents should I compare before filing ITR?
How do I check if my bond TDS is correct?
chunks.chunk: Users should reconcile bond income and TDS across the bank statement, Form 168 or Form 26AS, AIS where applicable, and platform reports. The bank statement verifies actual credits, payout dates, and net amounts. Form 168 verifies TDS deducted, deposited, and reported against the PAN. Platform reports help map repayment, sell, holding, and cashflow details.
chunks.answer_guidance: Give a practical checklist of records to compare and explain what each source verifies.

chunks.title: Advance tax or accrued entries across financial years
sample_questions: Why is my April TDS in the previous financial year?
Why does TDS deducted in May not match current year Form 168?
What should I do if Form 168 shows TDS in another year?
chunks.chunk: Some NBFCs may file year-end interest or payments as advance tax or accrued entries linked to 31 March. If a user checks in April or May and cannot find the TDS in the current financial year, they should also check the previous financial year's Form 168 for entries dated 31 March. Timing differences can occur because tax credits may be mapped to the earning period and not only the payment date.
chunks.answer_guidance: Guide the user to check the previous financial year and explain that this can be a timing issue. For unresolved cases, suggest internal escalation or document review.

chunks.title: Quarterly TDS reflection timeline
sample_questions: When will TDS reflect in Form 168?
What is the quarterly TDS filing timeline?
Why is my TDS not visible yet after payment?
chunks.chunk: TDS reflection in Form 168 is not instant. It depends on the deductor filing quarterly TDS returns and the return being processed. The PDF lists expected reflection around 15 August for Q1, 15 November for Q2, 15 February for Q3, and 15 June for Q4, assuming filing and processing are completed successfully.
chunks.answer_guidance: Mention that these are expected timelines and depend on successful deposit, correct PAN, filing, and TRACES processing.

chunks.title: Reasons TDS may be missing or delayed
sample_questions: Why is my TDS missing from Form 168?
What can delay TDS credit?
What should support check when TDS is not visible?
chunks.chunk: TDS may be missing or delayed if the deductor has not deposited tax, the PAN was entered incorrectly, the quarterly return has not been processed, there is a technical delay, the entry belongs to the previous financial year under the March 31 rule, or a correction return is pending. If TDS is still not reflected after checking the assessment year and timelines, the case may need internal escalation or Form 16A follow-up with the asset team.
chunks.answer_guidance: Provide a troubleshooting checklist and avoid promising immediate correction.

chunks.title: Tax statement disclaimer and reconciliation requirement
sample_questions: Can I rely only on the platform tax statement?
Is the tax report tax advice?
Should I reconcile the tax statement before filing?
chunks.chunk: The platform tax statement is for reference and convenience only and is not tax advice. Users should reconcile it with Form 26AS or Form 168 and their demat-linked bank account before filing ITR. Tax rates and structures may change, and actual tax liability can vary based on individual circumstances. Users should consult a qualified tax advisor or chartered accountant for validation.
chunks.answer_guidance: Use this disclaimer when users ask whether the report is final or sufficient for filing.

chunks.title: Master Report purpose and fields
sample_questions: What is the Master Report used for?
Which fields are in the Master Report?
How does the Master Report help tax filing?
chunks.chunk: The Master Report is a consolidated investment and taxation reference document showing bond holdings, repayments, transactions, and expected cash flows. It helps with portfolio tracking, tax filing support, income reconciliation, capital gains calculation, and future cash flow planning. Key fields include bond name, ISIN, units, invested amount, face value, acquisition cost, investment date, maturity date, XIRR, and interest or principal repayment frequency.
chunks.answer_guidance: Explain the report as a support document, not a standalone tax filing document.

chunks.title: Master Report tabs and tax filing mapping
sample_questions: Which Master Report tab helps with interest income?
Which report tab helps calculate capital gains?
How do Master Report tabs map to ITR?
chunks.chunk: The Master Report includes tabs such as Investment Summary, Repayment Summary, Sell Summary, Upcoming Cashflow Statement, and Holding Statement. For filing, Repayment Summary helps identify interest income and TDS, Sell Summary helps with capital gains or losses, Holding Statement is mainly for reference, Upcoming Cashflows is for estimation only, and Master Summary supports portfolio and acquisition reference.
chunks.answer_guidance: Map each tab to its filing use in plain language.

chunks.title: Taxation Report sections
sample_questions: What does the Taxation Report show?
Where do I find interest and TDS in the report?
Which section shows bonds sold?
chunks.chunk: The Taxation Report includes a summary section with user identity details such as name, PAN, email, and demat account; a Repayment Summary for interest paid, payment date, net amount received, and TDS; Maturity Details for bonds matured during the year; Bonds Sold for realised capital gains or losses; and a TDS Summary showing issuer-wise TDS deducted.
chunks.answer_guidance: Explain each section by what the user sees and how it supports filing or reconciliation.

chunks.title: How platform sections connect to ITR
sample_questions: Where do report sections go in ITR?
How do I map bond reports to tax filing?
Which report section is used for TDS credit?
chunks.chunk: Repayment Summary maps to income from other sources because it contains interest income. Bonds Sold maps to capital gains because it captures profit or loss on sale. TDS Summary maps to TDS credit because it shows tax already deducted. Maturity Details are mainly used as a cross-check to ensure no income or redemption detail is missed.
chunks.answer_guidance: Give a high-level mapping only and avoid giving line-by-line ITR form instructions unless asked.

chunks.title: Repayments Received report mapping
sample_questions: How do repayment items map to tax heads?
Is principal repayment taxable?
Where is accrued interest shown?
chunks.chunk: In the repayment and platform report mapping, coupon interest is taxable in the year it is paid or credited and falls under income from other sources. TDS on interest is tax credit after quarterly filing. Principal repayment is generally a non-taxable return of capital. Accrued interest at purchase is treated as part of acquisition cost, while accrued interest at sale may be taxed as interest in the year of sale. Capital gain or loss from sale is reported under capital gains.
chunks.answer_guidance: Use this when the user asks how platform rows map to Form 168, AIS, or tax heads.

chunks.title: April payout visible on platform but not Form 168
sample_questions: Why is my April payout not visible in Form 168?
The platform shows April TDS but Form 26AS does not. Why?
When will April payout TDS reflect?
chunks.chunk: April payouts fall under the Q1 filing cycle for April to June. The quarterly TDS filing date is July 31, and Form 168 or Form 26AS generally reflects the TDS only after the quarterly return is filed and processed. The platform may show TDS immediately based on the repayment date, creating a temporary mismatch.
chunks.answer_guidance: Explain the timing mismatch and expected Q1 filing cycle.

chunks.title: TDS after submitting Form 121
sample_questions: Why was TDS deducted after submitting Form 121?
Can Wint stop TDS after Form 121 submission?
Who processes Form 121?
chunks.chunk: TDS may still be deducted after submitting Form 121 if the NBFC has not accepted or processed the declaration. The PDF states that final acceptance and processing is at the NBFC's discretion, and Wint Wealth may have limited ability to intervene because it does not have access to the NBFC's internal systems.
chunks.answer_guidance: Set expectations gently and avoid guaranteeing reversal. Suggest checking issuer processing status where possible.

chunks.title: Capital loss shown on Wint tax report
sample_questions: Why am I seeing capital loss on Wint?
Why does the tax report show a loss?
Can premium purchase create loss in the report?
chunks.chunk: A user may see a capital loss in the Wint Tax Report if a bond was sold at a price lower than its investment amount or if the bond was purchased at a premium and redeemed at face value. The loss reflects the difference between acquisition cost and sale or redemption value, separate from interest income.
chunks.answer_guidance: Connect report loss to purchase cost versus sale or redemption value. Mention premium bonds as a common reason.

chunks.title: Accrued interest shown but not included in taxable income
sample_questions: Why is accrued interest shown but not taxable?
Why does the platform show accrued interest separately?
Why is accrued interest not included in taxable income?
chunks.chunk: Accrued interest may be shown on the platform for tracking or calculation purposes, but it is not necessarily included in taxable income until it is actually paid, credited, or settled in a taxable event such as sale. The taxable amount generally follows the actual interest payout or sale-related interest treatment, not merely the displayed accrued figure.
chunks.answer_guidance: Use this FAQ to explain platform display versus tax report inclusion.
